papers.title: statLens enables accurate and interpretable statistical intelligence
papers.abstract: Diverse existing approaches and analyses of large-scale biomedical omics datasets along with the complexity of the corresponding statistical analytical workflows pose challenges to the direct application of large language models (LLMs) to data analysis tasks. We present statLens, a model-agnostic AI-driven statistical intelligence framework that integrates LLMs, code and human review. We demonstrate statLens using differential expression analysis across heterogeneous biomedical data as a use case. On 102 benchmark tasks from 74 datasets across six omics modalities, statLens maintained consistently high accuracy (92.5--95.0%) across seven language models and outperformed LLM-only inference (17.5--46.8%), whereas autonomous-agent accuracy varied widely (58.7--99.5%). We also showed that statLens substantially improved the accuracy of the four small language models (92.5--94.4%) over autonomous agents (58.7--92.2%) and LLM-only inference (17.5--43.5%). By decomposing analytical workflows into complementary tasks for code, LLMs and human experts, statLens provides an integrated framework for more accurate, interpretable and reproducible AI-assisted data analysis, particularly in complex omics settings.

papers.title: SpaceMACE: Spatially-Aware Tumour Cell Annotation for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Accurate discrimination between tumour and non-tumour cells is essential for interpreting spatial transcriptomics data and identifying spatially resolved therapeutic targets. Existing tumour-cell annotation approaches were primarily developed for single-cell RNA sequencing and do not explicitly incorporate the spatial organization of cells. Here, we introduce SpaceMACE, an extension of the MACE tumour-cell annotation framework for sequencing-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics. SpaceMACE first combines reference-based cell-type classification with copy-number-variation-based tumour classification. The resulting consensus annotations are subsequently refined using spatial proximity and gene-expression similarity. We evaluated SpaceMACE across multiple spatial transcriptomics platforms, including Stereo-seq, Visium HD, CosMx and Xenium, and across colorectal, hepatocellular and ovarian cancer datasets. SpaceMACE retained the high precision of the original MACE framework while improving the spatial coherence of tumour-cell annotations. Together, these results demonstrate that SpaceMACE provides a scalable and platform-independent framework for tumour-cell annotation in spatial transcriptomics and supports the spatial investigation of tumour-specific molecular targets.

papers.title: Measuring Phylogenetic Information Content Based on Clade Support
papers.abstract: Phylogenetic information content is often understood as the degree to which data lend support to hypotheses about the monophyly of clades. This is most commonly expressed in terms of clade support, typically estimated by resampling techniques such as the bootstrap and the jackknife. Here, I discuss how to summarize this aspect of data quality. I show that raw bootstrap or jackknife proportions are unsuitable for this purpose and instead suggest a logarithmic transformation, which can be interpreted as translating the clade support values to the number of characters expected to give the same resampling proportion in parsimony analysis of a homoplasy-free data matrix. The distribution of the number of these "supporting characters" and descriptive statistics derived from this distribution, such as the mean (Mean Character Support, or MCS) and its standard deviation, provide powerful summaries of the quality of the underlying data set. I demonstrate for both empirical and simulated data sets that MCS accurately reflects information content, and that some popular alternative measures of data quality (the ensemble consistency index, the ensemble retention index, data decisiveness and the total support index) do not. Unlike most other measures of data quality, MCS can be applied to trees resulting from a range of alternative phylogenetic methods, including parsimony, distance and maximum likelihood approaches.

papers.title: Policy-Enforced Genomic Repositories and Institutional Data Governance for African Pathogen Surveillance with UbuntuBio
papers.abstract: Research centers curating pathogen sequence cohorts often operate under constrained bandwidth, multi-institutional data-sharing agreements, and strict biosafety requirements. Global public archives keep released sequences permanently open, external viral portals enforce terms outside local institutional custody, and standard Git Large File Storage (LFS) duplicates identical binaries across repositories without validating taxonomy or geography. We present UbuntuBio (v1.0.0), a Git-native, policy-enforced genomic repository platform deployed at https://ubuntubio.org and developed at the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), University of Ghana. UbuntuBio integrates four mechanisms under a single storage root: (1) bare Git repositories storing dataset cards, sample sheets, and approximately 130-byte LFS pointers backed by prefix-sharded SHA-256 content-addressed storage (CAS) with visibility-scoped wire deduplication; (2) a four-phase commit pipeline recoverable via cross-plane reconciliation that enforces 55 African Union country codes against offline Natural Earth polygons, core MIxS-derived fields, Taxon 9606 rejection, and server-keyed targeted human-marker screening identically across HTTP commits and Git pre-receive hooks; (3) institutional custody controls combining Data Use Agreements (DUAs), revocable 900-second RS256 capability tokens, key rotation, tamper-evident hash-chained logs, and externally anchorable RS256 audit checkpoints; and (4) an embedded SQLite WAL and FTS5 catalog filtered by access tier. In single-node evaluation, UbuntuBio classified 18/18 policy boundary fixtures consistently across Python, Git, and HTTP paths; showed 0/265,157 false cross-matches on 21/22 RefSeq pathogen sequences (while cross-matching Candida albicans 18S rDNA at 0.113% and Chlorocebus sabaeus Alu repeats in ENA stool reads, confirming targeted marker detection rather than verified human DNA decontamination); matched conditional uniform (n = 2,000; 200-seed 0.01% convergence 19.0% vs. 18.13% expected) and interior (n = 1,000) detection theory while detecting all spike-ins at [≥] 0.5% (30/30); halved two-repository disk usage on 613.83 MiB Nigerian E. coli runs; passed 27/27 structured-filter correctness checks over 10,000 biosamples and reached graded NDCG@10 = 0.920 on independent free-text BM25 queries with zero private leaks; and recovered cleanly across seven injected phase-transition faults.

papers.title: Generative Data Augmentation for Small-Cohort Glioblastoma Diagnosis from Circulating microRNA: Why Same-Modality Validation Overstates Performance
papers.abstract: Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have potential as minimally invasive biomarkers for glioblastoma (GBM), but the small size of discovery groups makes it difficult to develop a classifier. The discovery cohort, GSE122488, comprised 38 patients (n = 38). Generative data augmentation was applied to increase the dataset, although evaluations based on held-out samples from the same cohort or a single validation set make it difficult to distinguish biological signals from cohort- or platform-specific effects. CTGAN and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE) models were trained on the 38-patient cohort producing 500 synthetic samples each. Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were trained on augmented datasets and assessed using an escalating validation approach: first on an independent plasma cohort of the same modality (GSE184472, n = 118), and then on a tissue cohort from a different platform (Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA), n = 198). XGBoost using TVAE-augmented data achieved an AUROC of 0.59 (95% CI 0.49-0.70) on GSE184472, compared with 0.42 to 0.53 without augmentation, although no AUROC on this cohort was significantly different from chance. However, this improvement did not carry to CGGA, where AUROC was 0.40 (95% CI 0.32-0.48) before harmonisation and 0.47 after Min-Max harmonisation. After harmonisation, a recall of 1.00 resulted from predicting every sample as GBM, leading to an accuracy of 0.41 and showing poor discrimination. The generalisation gap was examined in terms of modality mismatch, differing class definitions between cohorts, synthetic-data-related class imbalance, and incomplete cross-platform harmonisation. These findings show the need for independent, cross-platform validation before using data augmentation for diagnosis. The escalating validation framework provides a way to evaluate generalizability in small-cohort studies.

papers.title: Deciphering the Biological Function of Tandem Mass Spectra Using a Dual-Modal Metabolite Language Model
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry untargeted metabolomics captures thousands of metabolic peaks from biological samples. Conventional identification-dependent metabolomics workflows require confident structural annotation before identified features can enter downstream pathway or functional analysis. However, only a small fraction of detected metabolic features can be assigned confident structural annotations, leaving a large fraction difficult to incorporate into downstream biological interpretation, a form of "functional dark matter". Here, we introduce Spec2Function, a function-centric framework that infers biological functions from tandem mass spectrometry (MS2) spectra. Spec2Function is trained using characterized spectrum-text pairs but does not require prior structural identification of the query spectra at inference time. At its core is Spec2Biotext, a dual-encoder contrastive model that embeds MS2 spectra and curated multi-aspect natural language functional texts into a unified functional space. Combined with a retrieval-augmented generation framework grounded in curated databases and biomedical literature, Spec2Function retrieves evidence-grounded biological knowledge and produces coherent functional summaries for individual spectra or groups of spectra. Across metabolite- and pathway-level benchmarks, Spec2Function achieved higher similarity to reference functional descriptions than the evaluated comparators and expanded the fraction of the metabolome accessible to functional interpretation. Application to a human liver cirrhosis cohort recapitulated known metabolic alterations and identified additional literature-supported functional modules. Applying Spec2Function to a 30-organ macaque aging atlas revealed organ-specific metabolic functions and previously unreported functional modules that were supported by independent human and mouse datasets. Together, these results position Spec2Function as a function-centric framework for scalable biological interpretation of structurally unannotated MS2 spectra.

papers.title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
papers.abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

papers.title: QT-RelCor: Statistical Inference for Comorbidity of Quantitative Traits and Disease from Related Individuals
papers.abstract: Background: Complex diseases with a high genetic component often cluster in families and are associated with quantitative traits (QT-s) such as endophenotypes showing comorbidity with the end-point disease trait. Detecting associations with such QT-s can provide a non-invasive approach to indicate disease onset at an early stage, or help in tracking disease severity. Traditional case-control studies generally involve unrelated individuals, which can introduce heterogeneity due to varying lifestyle and exposure patterns. Often QT values may be available from related individuals such as families of affected probands. In these situations, assessment of comorbidity restricting to unrelated cases and controls leads to unnecessary loss of power. On the other hand, ignoring the correlation structure of families leads to grossly incorrect confidence intervals impacting both type 1 error and power of tests. Yet, these practices are common in the absence of standard inference procedures for such data. Methods: We propose statistical procedures for analyzing clustered data to infer association between the QT-s and the binary trait. The methods allow a mix of families and unrelated cases and utilizes all available individuals. In particular, two novel competing approaches are proposed and evaluated: a parametric approach based on multivariate normal likelihood and a non-parametric approach that combines the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a modified version of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: We conducted simulation studies to assess type 1 error and power across multiple scenarios, which demonstrated the robustness of the proposed tests. Both the tests perform considerably better than both the classical t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test under both parametric and non-parametric settings. We illustrate the proposed methods by applying them on sibship data from the Centre for Brain and Mind program to identify a number of quantitative precursors significantly associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Conclusion: In summary, the proposed methods provide a robust and powerful approach to detect comorbid endophenotypes incorporating data from families of affected individuals. Findings from the analysis of sibling-based data on schizophrenia and bipolar disorder support role of a few selected neurocognitive assessments as potential markers of these disorders.

papers.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Missense Variant Pathogenicity Prediction in the KCNQ Gene Family
papers.abstract: Missense variants in the KCNQ family of voltage-gated potassium channel genes are associated with a broad spectrum of neurological and cardiac disorders for which computational tools capable of differentiating benign and pathogenic variants are essential. Here, we present, to our knowledge, the first application of quantum machine learning (QML) to missense pathogenicity prediction. We employ a hybrid quantum framework combining data re-uploading quantum neural networks with quantum support vector machines and applied it to pathogenicity classification across the full KCNQ gene family. Systematic exploration of circuit architectures revealed that optimal hyperparameter choices enable the proposed quantum model to achieve predictive performance superior to or comparable to state-of-the-art classical machine learning approaches, reaching AUC-ROC values of approximately 0.94 across the full dataset. Although no clear quantum advantage is observed at present, these results demonstrate that quantum feature representations can effectively capture biologically relevant patterns in variant data and establish QML as a viable framework for future applications in computational genomics and precision medicine.

papers.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
papers.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

papers.title: LDEN: Alternating projections for whole genome linkage disequilibrium estimation from next-generation sequencing data
papers.abstract: Viral populations often exist as quasispecies of closely-related variants with different mutations. Variants that possess combinations of mutations conferring an overall fitness advantage replicate preferentially. Understanding the true fitness effects of mutations involves disentangling the effects of individual mutations from their genetic background. This problem becomes particularly challenging due to linkage disequilibrium, the non-random association between mutations, which can cause neutral mutations to appear fit and vice versa. Viral populations are typically studied via next-generation sequencing, in which the read length is much shorter than the genome length, rendering long-range linkage disequilibrium unobservable. Estimation of linkage disequilibrium can be performed via population reconstruction, which reconstructs complete sequences before calculating linkage disequilibrium. However, this approach is computationally slow, memory-intensive, and prone to errors, particularly in regions of low coverage. In this work, we present a novel, population reconstruction-independent method for linkage disequilibrium estimation directly from next-generation sequencing data. Our approach uses the observed intra-read linkage disequilibrium values to estimate the unobservable inter-read ones by enforcing mathematical constraints on the linkage disequilibrium matrix. Specifically, because linkage disequilibrium quantifies the covariance between mutant allele frequencies, the linkage disequilibrium matrix must be positive semidefinite. We have formulated linkage disequilibrium estimation as a matrix completion problem and solve it via alternating projections on the constraints of positive semidefiniteness and observed linkage disequilibrium values. This allows the propagation of information from observed intra-read associations to the unobservable inter-read ones without reconstructing the individual variants. We demonstrate that our method yields higher accuracy while being two orders of magnitude faster compared to population reconstruction-based estimation. We demonstrate the performance of the method on both simulated as well as real data showing that it can estimate linkage disequilibrium from a variety of populations.

papers.title: FoldMapper: Protein Inverse Folding Model with Structure-Derived Evolutionary Profiles and a Multiscale Graph Encoder
papers.abstract: Protein inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences that fold into a target backbone structure. Existing deep-learning methods exploit backbone geometry but not evolutionary statistics. Those statistics come from a multiple sequence alignment, which must be built from a query sequence. That query is the sequence to be designed, so the dependency is circular. We present FoldMapper, an inverse folding model that breaks this circularity. It retrieves structural homologues by shape alone, then aggregates their amino-acid identities into a per-residue structural position-specific frequency (SPSF) profile. A Multiscale Graph Encoder passes a sparse profile-conditioned encoding into a dense structure-conditioned message-passing network. FoldMapper reaches 60.0% best-of-100 sequence recovery on TED domains, 64.9% on PDB, and 51.3%/53.1% on PPIBindBench non-peptide and peptide binders. Across both benchmarks, it lies on the recovery-diversity Pareto front. Structure self-consistency surpasses all baselines on RFdiffusion de novo monomer and binder backbones, and matches the strongest baselines on natural proteins. Ablations and profile-quality analyses show that structure itself encodes recoverable evolutionary information, accessible without a sequence homology search.

papers.title: DiGi: An Integer Programming Formulation for Diploid Genome Inference Using a Pangenome Reference
papers.abstract: Compared with genotyping against a single linear reference genome, pangenome-based genotyping enables more comprehensive detection of genetic variation, including structural variants. Existing genotyping methods employ a range of combinatorial, probabilistic, and statistical techniques. One class of methods formulates genotyping as a combinatorial path-finding problem in a pangenome graph, allowing bounded recombinations between reference haplotypes. By restricting solutions to mosaics of reference haplotypes, this formulation implicitly exploits linkage disequilibrium. However, extending this formulation to diploid genomes requires jointly identifying two mosaic paths, leading to an exponential increase in the search space. To address this challenge, we first represent the pangenome as a haplotype trellis graph, which maintains reference haplotypes as separate sequences and permits switching between them only at a predefined set of positions. Second, we formulate a combinatorial optimization problem that uses sequencing reads from a target genome to jointly infer a pair of haplotype paths in the graph. We then develop a probabilistic model that automatically sets the optimization parameters based on the read length and coverage of the input data, and an integer programming formulation to solve the resulting problem exactly. Our implementation, DiGi, successfully reconstructs both paternal and maternal copies of 90% of key HLA genes in target genomes absent from the pangenome reference, achieving sequence identity above 99.9%. On the HG002 Genome in a Bottle benchmark, DiGi achieves favorable F1 scores for genotyping SNVs, indels, and structural variants in the highly polymorphic major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region. DiGi remains accurate across a wide range of sequencing coverages, which makes it well suited to population-scale studies with variable coverage across samples.

papers.title: Segment Anything for Microscopy 2
papers.abstract: Foundation models have advanced microscopy image segmentation, but existing models are trained on two-dimensional data, struggle with complex structures in volumetric data, and address only a narrow range of analysis tasks. Here we present Segment Anything for Microscopy 2 (SAM2), a foundation model that adapts SAM2 to joint 2D and 3D segmentation in light and electron microscopy. Trained on annotations of more than 23 million cells and nuclei and 1.6 million cellular structures, SAM2 achieves state-of-the-art automatic and interactive segmentation and outperforms generalist and specialist methods on volumetric data. Dedicated models further enable accurate mitochondrion and nucleus segmentation in electron microscopy. Beyond segmentation, SAM2 supports pixel and object classification from few annotations as well as cell tracking in 2D and 3D time-lapse data. All functionality is available in the user-friendly SAM napari plugin. We demonstrated the capabilities of SAM2 on challenging use cases spanning developmental biology, organoid research, cardiac physiology, and histopathology.

papers.title: Pharmacophore-Inspired Virtual Receptor: Generating Realistic Peptide Binding Data for Machine Learning
papers.abstract: VReceptor is a virtual receptor simulation framework that generates realistic, sequence-dependent binding data for peptide-based therapeutics. It combines pharmacophore-inspired weighting schemes with amino acid similarity metrics to evaluate peptide design strategies in a controlled environment. Validation using the Prolactin-Releasing Peptide (PrRP) dataset confirms VReceptor's ability to approximate binding behaviours and optimize experimental planning. This framework empowers researchers in computational peptide design and active learning workflows while highlighting areas for further refinement.

papers.title: Sequence-based models predict TF binding with negligible contributions from motif cooperativity
papers.abstract: How transcription factors (TFs) selectively recognize their genomic targets among numerous sites containing similar DNA motifs remains an open question. Cooperative binding at neighboring motif sites is widely considered a key mechanism of TF specificity, yet its genome-wide contribution remains unclear. Machine learning models can now predict TF binding directly from DNA sequence, providing opportunities to investigate its underlying determinants. Here, we leveraged BPNet models trained on ~2,000 ENCODE TF binding profiles to systematically assess motif cooperativity. Although detected at individual loci, cooperativity made a negligible contribution to genome-wide binding predictions. Nevertheless, the models captured differences in binding preferences between TFs with similar motif preferences, even within the same cellular environment. These findings highlight the need to critically assess prevailing assumptions and explore alternative mechanisms underlying selective TF binding.

papers.title: Casanovo-TMT: deep learning-based de novo sequencing of TMTpro-labeled peptides and phosphopeptides
papers.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing reads peptides directly from tandem mass spectra, but none of the released deep learning models can sequence peptides labeled with isobaric tags such as TMTpro, which are widely used for multiplexed quantitative proteomics. We extended the residue vocabulary of Casanovo with TMTpro tags and phosphorylation, fine-tuned it on 21 million spectra from our laboratory, most of them TMTpro-labeled, and re-ranked the candidates in the beam by their agreement with the measured precursor mass. The resulting model, Casanovo-TMT, predicted the exact peptidoform for 84.7% of the TMTpro-labeled spectra in our test set and for 87.4 and 79.6% of the spectra in two public global-proteome datasets from other laboratories, whereas the extended vocabulary without fine-tuning gave 0.3%. Discarding the lowest-scoring predictions raised precision to 95% while retaining 81.7% of the test spectra. Casanovo-TMT also predicted the exact peptidoform for 69.2% of the spectra in a public phosphopeptide-enriched dataset and for 66 to 72% of the phosphopeptide spectra in three phosphoproteomic studies from our laboratory that were not used for training. In these studies, it identified numbers of phosphopeptides comparable to or larger than those of database search engines, and proportionally more where database search identified fewer. For the phosphopeptides identified only by Casanovo-TMT, entrapment estimated that more than 90% were correct, and an independent search engine assigned the same sequence to 95 to 98% of the spectra that it identified with confidence. Casanovo-TMT can therefore extend database search in TMTpro-based quantitative proteomics, particularly in studies in which database search identifies few phosphopeptides.

papers.title: SRAscout: Semantic discovery of public sequencing data through harmonized SRA and BioProject metadata
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of public sequencing data has created great opportunities for data-driven discovery in the life sciences, but it has also made it harder to find relevant datasets. The NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) hosts more than 45 million high-throughput sequencing runs, and the BioProject database, shared by NCBI, the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and the DNA Data Bank of Japan, describes the projects behind them. However, their metadata are often incomplete, inconsistently annotated and difficult to search using keywords alone. We present SRAscout, a web-based platform that enables semantic dataset retrieval by integrating SRA run metadata with the corresponding BioProject records. SRAscout collects and indexes metadata for about 714,000 BioProjects, and harmonizes sample attributes such as cell line, tissue, age, sex and treatment into a compact and consistent schema. For semantic embedding, SRAscout employs a biomedical sentence embedding model based on BioBERT, which generates dense vector representations from the title, name, organism and description of each project. Users can search in three modes, with the DOI or PubMed ID of an article, with free text, or with BioProject and SRA study accessions, and SRAscout finds the most related projects in each case. Free-text queries are processed through a hybrid of semantic and full-text search, which finds conceptually relevant studies even when different terms are used to describe the same biology, while exact terms such as gene names are still matched. Structured filters allow refinement by organism, assay type (for example RNA-seq and miRNA-seq), harmonized sample attributes such as tissue, cell type and disease, tag words, and many additional attributes. For each search, users can download a harmonized metadata table and ready-to-use scripts that fetch the sequencing files from ENA. SRAscout also offers a public API for programmatic access. By combining harmonized metadata with context-aware search in a single interface, SRAscout facilitates dataset discovery, meta-analysis and data reuse. The application is freely available at www.srascout.com.

papers.title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
papers.abstract: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

papers.title: A Biologically Interpretable Single-Cell Pathology Foundation Model for Molecular Decoding of H&E Images
papers.abstract: The microscopic structure of human tissues encodes molecular information that is not directly accessible by visual inspection. Current pathology foundation models improve histological interpretation but operate at multicellular resolution. It remains unclear whether routine histology contains structured molecular and cellular information recoverable at single-cell resolution, which biological properties are associated with this recoverability, and where its limits lie. Here, we introduce Loki2, a single-cell pathology foundation model trained on UniSeg, a pan-tissue resource integrating 15 million cells with segmentation, lineage annotations and measured or histology-inferred transcriptomic profiles. We examine the above question across cellular representation, molecular recoverability, and patient-level relevance. Loki2 captures cellular identity and continuous morphological variation, with interpretable latent dimensions linked to physical nuclear phenotypes through DAPI validation. Transcriptomic retrieval and in silico protein staining test molecular recoverability, with gene-level analyses revealing the strongest recovery for genes associated with morphologically distinct cellular identities and functions. Then, patient staging and biomarker discovery connect cellular morphology representations to clinical relevance. Together, these findings establish Loki2 as a biologically interpretable single-cell pathology foundation model and provide the opportunities of recovering cellular and molecular information from routine H&E histology at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Transferring CRISPRi knockdown responses to new cell lines requires screening part of each line
papers.abstract: Perturb-seq screens measure knockdown responses in one cell line at a time. Models that transfer responses to new lines rarely beat simple averages, and standard metrics often ignore noise. It is unclear how much of a response is shared and what a new line must contribute. We studied CRISPR interference Perturb-seq of essential genes in four human cell lines, using noise ceilings and calibrated metrics. We also introduce CASTER, a set-based model that adapts the transferred mean to the target line. After noise correction, responses correlated at a median of 0.52, highest between the TP53 wild-type lines. With 30% of a line screened, a linear model and CASTER scored 0.84 and 0.80 versus 0.44 for the transferred mean (1 equals a technical duplicate). CASTER led only at 2.5% screened (0.62 versus 0.47) and fell below the transferred mean without a screen. Response size tracked general essentiality more than line-specific dependency.

papers.title: Infernal-GPU: accurate E-values and sensitive covariance-model search for structured RNAs
papers.abstract: Covariance models (CMs) find structured RNAs by scoring sequence and base pairing together, and they underlie the Infernal software and the Rfam database. Their dynamic programming is expensive, so Infernal relies on two approximations: E-values are calibrated on a short stretch of random sequence, and fast sequence-only filters decide which parts of a target the CM examines. How much accuracy these approximations cost, and where, is largely unknown, because removing them on CPUs is prohibitively slow. We present Infernal-GPU, a GPU implementation of Infernal's CM dynamic programming that matches Infernal's results. Its key step evaluates the one serial recurrence of CM scoring, the self-loop of insert-left states, as two parallel prefix scans. One GPU calibrates all 4,227 Rfam models overnight, which makes calibrations on ten times more random sequence routine. These longer calibrations show that the E-values distributed with Rfam are off by more than twofold for one model in eight. An exhaustive search reference shows that sequence filters discard remote homologs whose similarity lies almost entirely in base pairing; behind permissive filters, Infernal-GPU recovers them with a third of the CPU work that Infernal needs at the same setting. Infernal-GPU is freely available at https://github.com/void-echo/infernal-gpu and from PyPI, together with Rfam 15.0 recalibrated on ten times more random sequence.

papers.title: Decompose and Recompose: Reference-Centered Multimodal Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Enzyme Turnover Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting enzyme turnover numbers ($k_{mathrm{cat}}$) from protein sequences and reaction chemistry helps prioritize candidates in virtual screening. Reliable ranking requires distinguishing activity differences between enzyme--reaction pairs. Recent interaction models combine enzyme and chemical information, but two representation challenges remain. First, reactants and products have distinct roles in catalysis: reactants are recognized and transformed, whereas products are formed and released. Yet these models merge the two sides before enzyme interaction, leaving the enzyme's response to each role implicit. Second, enzyme representations produced by cross-attention mix reaction-dependent changes with an enzyme-specific background shared across chemical conditions. This mixture can obscure activity-relevant differences between samples. To address these challenges, we introduce EnzRef, a lightweight multimodal framework that adapts frozen protein language models by decomposing reaction chemistry into reactant and product conditions, expressing each conditioned enzyme response relative to that enzyme's background, and recomposing the responses for activity prediction. Reference-Centered Cross-Attention uses each enzyme's average residue response as an internal reference to expose role-specific conditional deviations. Symmetry-Aware Semantic Recomposition encodes the mean deviation and directed role contrast into a joint activity representation. With 1.72M trainable parameters beyond the frozen encoder, EnzRef achieves state-of-the-art source-domain prediction on CatPred-DB and zero-shot transfer to TurNuP-DB. On unseen enzymes, it improves mean $R^2$ by 19.8% relative to MCKcat, the strongest baseline, without target-domain adaptation.

papers.title: Harmonized sample metadata and processed cortical and hippocampal transcriptomes from wild-type and Alzheimer's disease model mice
papers.abstract: Public mouse brain single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) datasets are difficult to reuse across studies because sample annotations are heterogeneous and incomplete. We harmonized sample-level metadata for 2,005 cortex and hippocampus samples from 389 studies, covering wild-type (WT) controls and Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related mouse models. Usable count data from 1,863 samples in 360 studies were uniformly processed into 12,628,942 cell and nuclear profiles with cell-type annotations. Expression-based indicators were consistent with the annotated sequencing protocol and sex, and integrated microglial profiles recovered established AD-associated signatures. To illustrate cross-study use, we asked whether microglial AD--WT expression differences varied with age and between cortex and hippocampus, using covariate-adjusted expression reconstructed with Kanade. Genes separated into groups with predominantly negative or positive AD--WT contrasts, including a group whose age-associated contrasts differed between cortex and hippocampus. These findings demonstrate the utility of harmonized metadata for investigating age- and region-dependent AD-associated transcriptional differences across studies. The resource supports explicit, reproducible cohort definitions across public mouse brain datasets.

papers.title: Optimal Predictivity of Random Signatures: Causes and Good Modeling Practices
papers.abstract: In high-throughput omics data, randomly-selected sets of markers ("signatures") have large and often optimal phenotypic predictivity. This creates problems of over-interpretation of biological and predictive importance of signatures, of bioinformatics algorithms and expert knowledge-driven selection. We conduct first an empirical study establishing that the phenomenon occurs across a variety of types of datasets/omics types and algorithms (224 combinations, >120 million models fitted). Random signatures are systematically reproducible across datasets. We develop a comprehensive theoretical framework, encompassing definitions, feasibility and impossibility theorems, and analytical formulas. The theory reveals as necessary and sufficient causes of these anomalous behaviors, the existence of large equivalence classes of optimally predictive feature sets, and their structure of information equivalences. We validate the theory with additional experiments and propose good practices intended to strengthen scientific rigor. Our findings apply to both algorithmic discovery and expert knowledge-driven signature selection, and to both existing and future algorithms and expert criteria. They also extend to all types of data with similar equivalence classes of optimal predictors.

papers.title: Chimeric and Outward Reads in Short-Read RNA Sequencing Data: A Unified Circular RNA Assembly Framework
papers.abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are RNA molecules that play important roles in regulating gene expression, yet detecting and assembling them from short read RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data remains challenging. Most methods rely on chimeric reads that cross the back-splicing junction (BSJ), but for lowly expressed circRNAs, these reads are often absent, so many circRNAs go undetected. In this work, we propose TERRACE 2.0, a method that addresses this limitation by leveraging an additional but underutilized signal: outward reads. These are paired-end reads that point away from each other when aligned to the reference genome, which is a direct consequence of sequencing a fragment from a circRNA. Together, this multi-signal framework enables circRNAs to be detected and assembled more accurately from short-read RNA-seq data. TERRACE 2.0 infers candidate BSJs from outward reads by testing which ones give a fragment length consistent with the library, reconstructs each full-length circRNA from a splice graph, and combines outward and chimeric reads in a single representation that selects among the candidates jointly. On eight human tissue samples, TERRACE 2.0 has the best average F-score with and without gene annotations. On an alignment that retains more chimeric reads, it is the most accurate assembler in every sample, while its predecessor TERRACE loses much of its precision. Most notably, outward reads are involved in 36% to 56% of the true circRNAs that TERRACE misses, and on simulated data TERRACE 2.0 also has the highest recall and F-score.

papers.title: Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG) for Antiviral and Antibacterial Drug Discovery.
papers.abstract: Infectious diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, while therapeutic discovery is hindered by fragmented biomedical data and antimicrobial resistance. To address this challenge, we developed the Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG), a queryable platform that integrates curated chemical, biological, pharmacological, and clinical information relevant to infectious-disease drug discovery. Using a customized ORION pipeline, we integrated 20 data sources, including DrugCentral, SMACC, Heli-SMACC, NPASS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and host-virus interaction databases, into a Neo4j graph containing more than 4.6 million nodes and 26 million edges. IDKG supports graph-based reasoning through Clinical Outcome Pathways (COPs) and incorporates curation workflows for small molecules, biologics, and complex mixtures. Illustrative applications include reconstruction of a literature-supported remdesivir pathway for COVID-19 and graph-based mechanistic interpretation of experimentally observed quorum-sensing inhibitor-antibiotic synergies in multidrug-resistant bacteria. The platform provides an interoperable framework for drug repurposing, target prioritization, and mechanism-based hypothesis generation. IDKG is freely available at https://idkg.mml.unc.edu.

papers.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Performance, Interpretability, and Cross-Database Redundancy
papers.abstract: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) classifiers are typically developed and evaluated within a single curated database, leaving open how much two independently curated databases agree and what that implies for apparent cross-database generalization. We trained an XGBoost classifier on amino acid trigram frequencies and physicochemical descriptors using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), the field's largest curated ARG resource. The model separated resistance genes from non-resistance proteins with near-ceiling accuracy (AUROC = 0.982, MCC = 0.886); a label-shuffling null baseline collapsed to chance (AUROC = 0.508) and bootstrap confidence intervals were narrow, confirming genuine signal rather than data leakage or overfitting. SHAP analysis attributed this performance to biologically interpretable features, notably the trigram KTG, isoelectric point, and aromaticity, each consistent with known catalytic motifs in resistance enzymes. Before testing the classifier against ResFinder, one of CARD's most widely used counterparts, we assessed database independence by clustering sequences with CD-HIT, finding that 96.8-98.7% of ResFinder sequences shared substantial protein identity with CARD even at a permissive 50% identity threshold, indicating the two databases largely represent the same sequence population, with direct implications for how cross-database generalization should be measured. On the small subset of ResFinder sequences genuinely non-redundant with CARD (40-100 sequences, depending on threshold), the classifier failed completely, never classifying any as resistance genes; SHAP traced this failure to sequence length, as non-redundant sequences are nearly three times longer than training proteins, and length is among the model's most influential features. The same pattern emerged by resistance mechanism: the model achieved perfect accuracy on beta-lactamases, compact single-domain enzymes well represented in training (100%, n = 351), but correctly identified only 38.5% of efflux pump components (n = 13), a mechanism built from large, multi-domain transporters rather than compact catalytic enzymes. Together, these results describe a capable, interpretable ARG classifier alongside a quantified methodological caution: cross-database redundancy must be measured rather than assumed, and when a sequence-composition classifier fails, the failure is often explained by protein architecture rather than database origin.

papers.title: GatorAnchor: Cross-Modal Uncertainty-Aware Learning of Reliable Cell Neighborhoods in Single-Cell Multi-Omics
papers.abstract: Cross-modal uncertainty challenges single-cell multi-omics integration because molecular modalities differ in sparsity, technical noise, and context-dependent biological informativeness, producing discordant cell-cell relationships. Treating conflicting evidence as equally reliable can propagate uncertain relationships and obscure biologically meaningful cellular heterogeneity. GatorAnchor is a cross-modal uncertainty-aware framework that learns modality-specific probabilistic representations, quantifies disagreement across modalities and neighborhood evidence sources, and refines cell-cell relationships according to their reliability. Across ten paired transcriptome-protein and transcriptome-chromatin datasets, GatorAnchor achieves the highest mean performance across four evaluation metrics among nine representative integration methods, demonstrating improved resolution of cellular heterogeneity. Candidate relations with greater composite unreliability show lower consistency with reference cell-type structure, whereas filtering highly unreliable relations increases same-type edge purity across all datasets. Modality conflict is associated with transcript-protein measurement discordance, while transcriptome-chromatin analyses reveal lineage-dependent contributions of molecular and decoder-derived evidence. A three-modality transcriptome-chromatin-protein analysis characterizes cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4)-related communities with distinct molecular profiles and consistent within-donor contrasts across 12 donors. Under incomplete and mosaic measurements, GatorAnchor preserves informative cell-population structure, while cross-modal correspondence increasingly depends on paired-cell anchors. These findings support uncertainty-aware neighborhood refinement for reliable and interpretable characterization of cellular heterogeneity.

papers.title: Diffusion geometry and topology reveal Alzheimer's proteomic states
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial molecular heterogeneity. Identifying biologically distinct proteomic states may improve understanding of disease heterogeneity and support precision diagnostics. METHODS: Cerebrospinal fluid proteomic data from ADNI were analyzed. Among 6,361proteins tested between cognitively normal and AD groups, 407 remained significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction (FDR < 0.05), with 404 retained after missingness filtering. Following preprocessing and outlier removal, 130 individuals were included. Diffusion geometry and persistent homology were applied to characterize intrinsic proteomic structure without predefined clusters. The framework was further evaluated in an independent mass spectrometry cohort. RESULTS: Persistent homology revealed multiscale organization of the AD proteomic landscape. At the selected H0 filtration scale, two dominant proteomic states (n = 71 and n = 42) contained most individuals, alongside smaller components. H1 persistence identified nontrivial cyclic structure, indicating continuous higher-order organization beyond discrete state partitions. The dominant states exhibited distinct proteomic profiles and differed substantially in tau-related biomarkers. Elevated tau pathology in one state was reproduced in the independent cohort, whereas A{beta}42 differences were less consistent across cohorts. DISCUSSION: AD proteomic heterogeneity is characterized by multiscale organization combining dominant group structure with continuous higher-order relationships.
